title: When you miss a day
hookLine: in a 2009 study, missing one day didn't derail a forming habit (Lally et al.)
tomorrow: Camp 3 close: the practice is yours

cards: It will happen. Maybe not this week or this month, but one day you'll miss. Not even the one-breath version.
You'll get to bedtime and realize the whole day went by without a single practice. Then comes the dangerous part, and it isn't the missed day. It's the voice afterward.
Well, that's ruined. I always do this. I'm just not a person who sticks with things.
That voice can end a good habit faster than any busy day. So meet it now, while things are calm.

teach.b: In 2009, a team at University College London led by Phillippa Lally followed ninety-six volunteers for twelve weeks.
Each picked one new daily habit, like a glass of water with lunch or a short run before dinner, and reported every day how automatic it felt. Two findings stand out.
First, it took much longer than the twenty-one days you sometimes hear.

The typical time to something like automatic was about sixty-six days, and for some people far longer. So if you still have to remember your practices on purpose, you're not failing. You're on schedule.
Second, the one to keep: missing a single day did not meaningfully set people back.
The habit curve kept climbing. What breaks the chain is the story told about the gap. If one missed day becomes proof you're hopeless, you stop.
If it's just a missed day, you start again tomorrow. You already know how.
Back on day one hundred, counting breaths, the instruction was: when you lose count, start again at one. No scolding, no starting over as a person.
And Seneca, reviewing his day, ended with: see that you don't do it again; this time I forgive you. So restart without a speech. No apology, no big plan to make up for it, no doubling up tomorrow.
Just do today's practice, today. The missed day is already behind you. The next breath isn't.

how: Habit researchers and coaches usually advise treating a missed day as a small gap rather than a failure, and simply resuming the next day without trying to make up for it.

games.why: just start again. in the 2009 study, one missed day didn't derail the habit; the story about the gap is what does.

practice: Imagine it's the morning after a missed day, and notice the voice getting ready to give its speech. Let it start, then gently cut it off and just begin: one breath, the first of your five, and feel how light that is.
Keep breathing, starting again at one whenever your mind wanders.

wordCard.voice: Habit curve, the gradual rise researchers found toward a habit feeling automatic, which one missed day doesn't meaningfully set back. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: just start again. No speech, and no making up for it. Until tomorrow, then.

sources.ref: Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle (2009), How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world, European Journal of Social Psychology 40(6)
